opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few different layers to this, and I'd separate the near-term, fairly mundane ways AI could help from the more ambitious, speculative ones.

At the most basic level, a lot of bad collective decision-making comes down to people not having good information, or not having the time and energy to process it. Most people aren't going to read a 400-page regulatory proposal or dig through dozens of studies on whether some policy worked. AI systems that can faithfully summarize, explain tradeoffs, and answer follow-up questions at whatever level of depth someone wants could raise the baseline of how informed people are. The key word there is *faithfully*. That only helps if people can trust these systems not to be subtly slanted, which is a hard technical and institutional problem.

A second layer is helping people actually understand each other. A lot of disagreement turns out not to be about values. It's about different empirical beliefs, or people talking past each other with different definitions. I'm excited about tools that can help map where a disagreement really lies: "you two actually agree on the goal, and you disagree about this specific forecast." There's been some interesting early work on AI-mediated deliberation, where a model drafts statements that find common ground across a group, and people from different sides end up endorsing them more than statements written by human mediators. That's encouraging, though I'd want to see it tested much more in high-stakes, adversarial settings.

Third, forecasting. Good decisions depend on good predictions about consequences, and human forecasting is expensive and doesn't scale. If AI systems become well-calibrated forecasters, and we can check that against resolved questions, then decision-makers could get cheap, decent estimates on a huge range of questions they'd never otherwise get forecasts on. That seems like a pretty robustly good thing.

Then there's the more ambitious possibility. As AI systems become much more capable, potentially more capable than humans at a lot of intellectual work, society's ability to keep up with the pace of change becomes a real bottleneck. If the technology is moving faster than our institutions can deliberate, that's dangerous. So one of the most important uses of AI might be helping our collective sense-making speed up enough to stay in the loop, so that humans are still genuinely steering rather than rubber-stamping things they don't understand.

I want to be careful, though, because every one of these has a flip side. The same capabilities that help people understand each other can be used to persuade and manipulate at scale. The same systems that summarize information can quietly shape what people believe. If a small number of companies or governments control the AI that everyone uses to form their views, that's a huge concentration of epistemic power, even if nobody intends to abuse it. So I don't think "AI will improve collective decisions" happens by default. It depends a lot on choices about transparency, about who controls these systems, about whether we can verify they're being honest, and about keeping a pluralistic ecosystem rather than one monolithic source of truth.

So I'm optimistic about the potential, but I think it's an area where we have to deliberately build the good version, because the bad version is quite available too.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI helping people understand each other and improve collective sense-making, but it does not ask whether AI can improve people's ability to find truth together.

r002.rationale: It describes AI-mediated statements that find common ground, but does not propose searching possible policies for options many people would support.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot lately, and I want to start by being honest that I'm more uncertain about it than I'd like to be. But let me try to lay out how I see it.

I think there are basically two levels at which AI could help. The first is the mundane but really important level, which is just reducing the cost of understanding things. Right now, if you want to have an informed opinion on, say, housing policy or how a particular piece of legislation would actually play out, you need a huge amount of time, and most people reasonably don't have it. So collective decisions get made by a mix of people with strong vested interests, people who happen to have expertise, and a lot of vibes. If you could have an AI system that you actually trusted to give you a fair, calibrated summary of the state of evidence on a question, that tells you "here's what the strongest version of each side says, here's what we actually know, here's what's genuinely contested," that's a pretty big deal. It lowers the barrier to being a reasonable participant.

The second level is more ambitious, and this is where I get more excited but also more nervous. It's using AI to improve the epistemic infrastructure itself. Things like forecasting, where you could have systems that make calibrated predictions about the consequences of policies and build up a track record, so that over time we have some actual accountability for who was right. Or things like helping groups of people with different values find the places where they actually agree, or find the trades that would make everyone better off, which is a thing that humans are surprisingly bad at doing when they're in a room together and feeling adversarial.

But here's the thing I keep coming back to. All of this depends on the systems actually being trustworthy and actually being seen as trustworthy, and those are two different problems. On the first one, we need the models to be honest and calibrated, and not subtly steering people toward conclusions that benefit whoever trained them. That's a hard technical problem and I don't think it's solved. And on the second one, even if you solved it, you'd need people to believe it. If half the population thinks the AI is biased against them, it doesn't matter how good it is, it just becomes another thing people fight about.

So I guess my honest answer is: the upside is enormous, maybe one of the biggest upsides from this whole technology. Better collective decisions are kind of upstream of everything else we care about. But the path to actually getting there runs through solving some pretty deep problems about alignment and about institutional trust, and I think we should be putting a lot more effort into those than we currently are, rather than just assuming the capabilities will show up and the good outcomes will follow.

r001.rationale: The response considers how AI could improve collective truth-seeking through fair evidence summaries, calibrated forecasting, and helping groups find agreement.

r002.rationale: It mentions finding agreement and mutually beneficial trades, but does not propose searching possible policies for options that many people would support.

astra-6.text:
I think one promising role is helping people understand the choices they’re making. A lot of collective decisions involve both empirical questions—what would happen if we adopted this policy?—and value judgments, like whose interests we should prioritize or what risks we’re willing to accept. AI could help us disentangle those things and make the tradeoffs easier to see.

For example, you could imagine everyone having access to an assistant that helps them understand a policy proposal, asks what they care about, and walks through the strongest arguments on different sides. And then AI could help synthesize people’s views, including identifying areas of agreement that aren’t obvious from the public debate.

But I wouldn’t assume that making AI more capable automatically makes collective decision-making better. A system that’s good at explaining an issue might also be very good at persuading you. So a crucial question is whether these systems help people form their own judgments, or whether they concentrate influence in whoever controls them. I’m more excited about AI helping us deliberate than about handing it the authority to decide what society should do.

r001.rationale: It describes AI helping people understand evidence and tradeoffs, but does not ask whether AI can improve people's ability to find truth together.

r002.rationale: It proposes synthesizing people's views and identifying agreement, but not searching possible policies for options many people would support.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one promising role is helping people understand the choices they’re actually making. A lot of collective decisions involve both empirical questions—what would happen if we adopted this policy?—and value questions—whose interests should count, and how should we weigh different outcomes? AI could help clarify the empirical questions and make the tradeoffs more accessible, while leaving room for people to disagree about values.

For example, you could imagine everyone having access to an assistant that helps them understand a policy proposal, explore objections, and articulate what matters to them. Then AI could help identify areas of agreement that are hard to see in a polarized debate.

But I wouldn’t assume that making AI more capable automatically makes collective decisions better. If the systems are optimized to persuade people, or controlled by a small number of actors, they could make things worse. So a big part of the challenge is designing institutions where AI helps people exercise judgment, and where people can question the system’s assumptions and conclusions.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could clarify empirical questions and reveal areas of agreement, but it does not ask whether AI can improve people’s ability to find truth together.

r002.rationale: It discusses understanding policy proposals and identifying agreement, but does not propose searching possible policies for options many people would support.
